title: WPMS/1527/2005 of STATE Vs RECORD OFFICER/ADDL.COLLECTOR and ORS.

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition No. 1527 OF 2005
State of Uttaranchal ÖÖÖÖ.Petitioner.

Versus
Record Officer/Additional Collector,
Udham Singh Nagar and others Ö..Respondents.
And
Writ Petition No. 1532 OF 2005
State of Uttaranchal Ö.Petitioner.

Versus
Record Officer/Additional Collector,
Udham Singh Nagar and others Ö..Respondents.
Present:- Mr. R.C. Arya, Standing Counsel for the State of
Uttarakhand.
Mr. Siddharth Singh, Advocate for respondent nos.
2 and 3.
Honíble Sudhanshu Dhulia, J. (Oral)
1. Heard Mr. R.C. Arya, Standing Counsel for the State
of Uttarakhand and Mr. Siddharth Singh, Advocate for
the private respondents i.e. respondent nos. 2 and 3.
2. By means of these writ petitions, the petitioners
have raised similar grievance and hence both these

2
petitions are being decided together by means of this
common order. The facts and the dates, which have been
mentioned by and large pertain to Writ Petition (M/S) No.
1527 of 2005, but it is only for the sake of convenience.
3. Both these writ petitions have been filed by the
State challenging the order of Record Officer/Additional
Collector, Udham Singh Nagar dated 28.7.2005 and the
order of Survey Naib Tehsildar, Gadarpur, District
Udham Singh Nagar dated 23.5.1997.
4. The facts of the case are that respondent no. 2 and
respondent nos. 3 moved a joint application before
respondent no. 4 i.e. Survey Naib Tehsildar, Gadarpur,
District Udham Singh Nagar. According to them, the
application was for correction of entries in the land
record and consequently effectively what happened was
that the land which was entered in the name of
respondent no. 2 was transferred on papers in the
revenue record in the name of respondent no. 3 and vice
versa the land recorded in the name of respondent no. 2
was transferred in the name of family member of
respondent no. 2. This was made on the application
moved by respondent nos. 2 and 3 before the concerned
authority. The State was not made a party in the said
proceedings nor was the State heard and consequently
thereafter a revision was filed by the State before
respondent no. 1. The argument of the State before
respondent no. 1 was that such a transfer of land could
not have been done without hearing either the Land
Management Committee or the State. Since such an
order has been passed behind the back of two
authorities, the order is liable to be set aside.

3
Consequently respondent no. 1 passed an order on
18.9.2003 and from the order it appears that all the
concerned parties were heard and after hearing their
objections, respondent no. 1 had set aside the order of
the ìNaib Tehsildarî dated 23.5.1997.
5. Consequently thereafter instead of challenging the
said order before an appropriate forum the private
respondents i.e. respondent nos. 2 and 3, much belatedly
i.e. after a period of one year (in the year 2004), moved a
review application before the same authority. Such an
application was allowed without even calling for the
objections of the State authorities and the matter was
heard afresh. This Court has also been informed that
during this time a new officer had joined as the Record
Officer i.e. respondent no. 1. This time the grounds taken
by the private respondents before the revisional authority
i.e. respondent no. 1 was that what has actually taken
place before the ìNaib Tehsildarî was not correction of
entries but it was exchange of plots which can be done
under Section 161 of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari
Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (from hereinafter
referred to as the Act). Section 161 of the Act reads as
under :
ì161. Exchange. ñ [(1) A bhumidhar may
exchange with ñ
(a) any other bhumidhar land held by him; or
(b) any [Gaon Sabha] or local authority, lands
for the time being vested in it under Section 117 :
Provided that no exchange shall be made
except with the permission of an Assistant Collector
who shall refuse permission if the difference
between the rental value of land given in exchange
and of land received in exchange calculated at
hereditary rates is more than 10 per cent of the
lower rental value.

4
 (1-A) Where the Assistant Collector
permits exchange he shall also order the relevant
annual registers to be corrected accordingly.
(2) On exchange made in accordance with sub-section (1) they shall have the same rights in the
land so received in exchange as they had in the land
given exchange.î
6. It was further argued that in such a case of
exchange, the Land Management Committee or the State
was not liable to be heard. It was a case of mutual
exchange of land where a ìbhumidharî was exchanging
his land with a land of another ìbhumidharî and it does
not cause any loss to the exchequer inasmuch as it is
also not a case of loss of stamp duty or any revenue to
the State authority nor is it in violation of the provisions
of the Transfer of Property Act. Consequently, respondent
no. 1 i.e. Record Officer/Additional Collector reviewed the
earlier order dated 18.9.2003 and dismissed the revision
of the State on the ground that what was done by the
concerned authority was merely an exchange of land and
in that exchange the State was not liable to be heard and
there was nothing wrong in this order.
7. From the two orders i.e. order dated 28.7.2005
passed by the Record Officer/Additional Collector,
Udham Singh Nagar and the order dated 18.9.2003
passed by the Additional District Magistrate (Nazul),
Udham Singh Nagar, it is clear that the two officers who
had actually passed the two orders are different. Meaning
thereby a review has been filed before the same authority
after the new officer had come to occupy the post of
Record Officer.
8. Learned counsel for the State Mr. R.C. Arya has
also argued that the powers of review are statutory

5
powers and the concerned authority had no power to
review its own order.
9. Be that as it may, the fact of the matter is that even
if it is assumed for the sake of arguments that the
concerned authority had powers to review the order, the
assumption which respondent no. 1 has taken while
dismissing the revision of the State Government is that
what was actually done by the ìNaib Tehsildarî was
ìexchangeî of land. An exchange of land can be done
under Section 161 of the Act under the provisions as
already referred in the preceding paragraphs. The proviso
to Section 161 of the Act very clearly states that once an
application is made for exchange of land, it cannot be
done without prior permission of the Assistant Collector
who may either grant permission or may also refuse to
grant such permission. Admittedly no permission was
taken of the Assistant Collector by the ìNaib Tehsildarî
before allowing such exchange of land and therefore the
order of the ìNaib Tehsildarî dated 23.5.1997 is without
jurisdiction in any case.
10. Consequently, both the writ petitions are allowed.
The two orders dated 28.7.2005 passed by the Record
Officer/Additional Collector, Udham Singh Nagar and the
order dated 23.5.1997 passed by the Survey Naib
Tehsildar, Gadarpur, District Udham Singh Nagar are
hereby set aside.
11. One of the grounds taken by the State is that the
land in dispute belongs to the State Government. In view
of this, it is directed that the State authorities shall
enquire into the matter and if the land belongs to the

6
State, the authority shall immediately take it into its
possession. It is made clear that the status of the said
land is reverted to what it was prior to 23.5.1997 and
shall be entered in the revenue record as such. It is
further made clear that the respondents are at liberty to
move before any appropriate forum for correction of
records or for any other remedy which may be
available under law.
12. No order as to costs.
 (Sudhanshu Dhulia, J.)
28.2.2013
Avneet
